result: Post-training memantine (MEM) treatment enhances forgetting of recent contextual fear memory in a dose-dependent manner, correlating with increased hippocampal neurogenesis. The MEM-4 group showed significantly reduced freezing at Test 2 compared to vehicle controls, with no spontaneous recovery observed. A significant negative correlation was found between BrdU-positive cells (neurogenesis marker) and forgetting in the MEM-25 group.
evaluation: Claims C2-C11, C46-C47 provide converging evidence from behavioral data (Figures 1A-B), neurogenesis quantification (Figures 1C-D), and correlational analysis (Figure 1E). The dose-dependent effect, lack of spontaneous recovery, and correlation between neurogenesis and forgetting collectively support this result. Statistical significance is reported for key comparisons.

result: MEM-induced forgetting is specific to hippocampus-dependent memories. MEM enhanced forgetting of hippocampus-dependent inhibitory avoidance memory but failed to promote forgetting of amygdala-dependent cued fear memory.
evaluation: Claims C13-C18, C48 demonstrate regional specificity through two complementary behavioral tasks (Figures 2A-B). The inhibitory avoidance task (hippocampus-dependent) showed MEM effects while cued fear conditioning (amygdala-dependent) did not. This pattern is consistent with neurogenesis occurring primarily in hippocampus and supports the mechanistic hypothesis.

result: MEM enhances forgetting even when fear memory is strong (induced by 10 foot shocks), with no spontaneous recovery observed.
evaluation: Claims C19-C20 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2C showing significant reduction in freezing at Test 2 despite high initial freezing levels (>60%), and absence of spontaneous recovery at the Sp. Test. This extends the generalizability of MEM-induced forgetting beyond weak memories.

result: MEM treatment fails to enhance forgetting of remote (8-week-old) contextual fear memory when administered without reminders, consistent with remote memories becoming hippocampus-independent over time.
evaluation: Claims C21-C22, C49, C99-C100 are supported by experimental data (Figure 2D) showing no difference between MEM and vehicle groups when treatment begins 8 weeks post-training. This is consistent with systems consolidation theory (supported by multiple citations) and sets up the critical test of whether reminders can restore hippocampal dependence.

result: Long (10 min) but not short (3 min) context re-exposure 8 weeks after training renders remote contextual fear memory susceptible to MEM-induced forgetting. The MEM group with 10 min re-exposure showed significantly less freezing than all other groups.
evaluation: Claims C23-C26, C51, C106 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3A showing duration-dependent effects of reminders. Only the 10 min re-exposure + MEM group showed significant forgetting. This is a central finding demonstrating that remote memories can be made vulnerable to neurogenesis-induced forgetting through appropriate reminders.

result: Exercise (running wheel access) following long (10 min) but not brief (3 min) context re-exposure promotes forgetting of remote contextual fear memory, replicating the MEM effect with an alternative neurogenesis enhancer.
evaluation: Claims C27-C29, C52 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3B and citations establishing exercise as a neurogenesis enhancer. The parallel findings with exercise and MEM strengthen the conclusion that neurogenesis enhancement (rather than drug-specific effects) drives forgetting after long reminders.

result: Long (but not brief) reminders render remote contextual fear memories susceptible to forgetting induced by treatments that increase hippocampal neurogenesis (MEM or exercise).
evaluation: Claims C30, C58, C87 represent summary conclusions supported by the combined evidence from Figures 3A-B showing convergent effects of two different neurogenesis enhancers (MEM and exercise) following long but not short reminders. This is a key integrative finding of the study.

result: Long (10 min) but not short (3 min) context re-exposures induce hippocampus-dependent reconsolidation of remote fear memory, as demonstrated by sensitivity to protein synthesis inhibition (anisomycin) in the hippocampus.
evaluation: Claims C31, C33-C36, C60, C109 are supported by anisomycin (ANI) infusion experiments (Figures 4A-C). ANI impaired memory after 3 min re-exposure at 24 hr (recent memory) and after 10 min re-exposure at 4 weeks (remote memory), but not after 3 min re-exposure at 4 weeks. This demonstrates duration-dependent reconsolidation of remote memories.

result: Long (10 min) but not short (3 min) context re-exposures activate c-fos expression in the hippocampus at remote time points. In hippocampal CA1 and CA3, brief re-exposure induced c-fos at recent but not remote time points, while longer re-exposures induced c-fos at both delays.
evaluation: Claims C37-C42, C62, C69, C108 are supported by c-fos immunohistochemistry data (Figure 5A-B). The differential pattern of hippocampal activation (long but not short reminders at remote time points) provides molecular evidence that extended reminders re-engage the hippocampus for remote memories. The ACC showed the opposite pattern, consistent with systems consolidation.

result: Retrieval of remote memory becomes hippocampus-dependent 24 hr after long (10 min) context re-exposure, as demonstrated by lidocaine-induced hippocampal inactivation impairing retrieval at Test 1 but not Test 2 (drug-free).
evaluation: Claims C43-C45, C64, C110-C111 are supported by lidocaine inactivation data (Figure 5C). The temporary impairment at Test 1 (with drug) but normal performance at Test 2 (drug-free) demonstrates that hippocampal activity is required for retrieval 24 hr after long re-exposure, supporting the hypothesis that remote memories return to a hippocampus-dependent state.

result: The 10 min re-exposure does not trigger extinction of remote contextual fear memory, but rather reconsolidation, based on: (1) decreased freezing only with neurogenesis enhancers, (2) duration requirements differing from extinction, and (3) presence of hippocampal c-fos expression (characteristic of reconsolidation, not extinction).
evaluation: Claims C53-C57 provide multiple lines of reasoning and evidence distinguishing reconsolidation from extinction. The treatment-dependence (C54), duration requirements (C55), and c-fos expression pattern (C56-C57) collectively support this interpretation. However, the claim relies partly on unpublished data and inference rather than direct experimental tests of extinction.

result: Extended context re-exposures enable remote memory to return to a hippocampus-dependent state by reactivating the hippocampus, thereby allowing enhanced forgetting by increases in hippocampal neurogenesis. This represents the central mechanistic hypothesis of the study.
evaluation: Claims C59, C61, C63, C65, C70 represent the integrative hypothesis supported by converging evidence from reconsolidation (ANI experiments), molecular activation (c-fos), functional dependence (lidocaine), and behavioral forgetting (MEM/exercise). The multiple independent lines of evidence provide strong support for this mechanistic model.

result: Prior research established that remote memory can be recalled under conditions of retrograde amnesia (unlike recent memory), and that hippocampal immediate early gene expression occurs during retrieval of recent but not remote memory with brief re-exposures.
evaluation: Claims C66-C68 accurately summarize prior literature (multiple citations) establishing the standard view of systems consolidation. These claims provide important context for the current findings showing that long re-exposures can reverse this pattern. The citations appear appropriate and the characterization is consistent with the field.

result: Reconsolidation serves to maintain, enhance, and/or update memory. The authors' prior work showed that reconsolidation of recent memory occurs after 3 min re-exposures, while remote memory reconsolidation requires longer (10 min) re-exposures and hippocampal reactivation.
evaluation: Claims C71-C76 accurately cite prior literature on reconsolidation function (C71) and the authors' previous findings (C72-C74). Claim C75 is supported by current data (c-fos expression). Claim C76 is speculative about memory updating but appropriately qualified. These claims provide important context and interpretation.

result: Hippocampal neurogenesis enhancers (MEM and running) did not completely abolish fear memories, showing residual freezing. However, this residual freezing is comparable to that observed in other memory disruption studies, and c-fos expression data (unpublished) suggests genuine forgetting rather than intact memory.
evaluation: Claims C77-C82 address an important limitation (incomplete memory erasure) but rely partly on unpublished c-fos data (C81) and comparisons to prior literature (C79). While the reasoning is plausible and the comparison to other studies is appropriate, the unpublished data and speculative nature of C78 introduce uncertainty. The conclusion (C80, C82) may be overstated given the evidence.

result: Forgetting of fear memory through increases in neurogenesis permanently erases fear responses (no spontaneous recovery), in contrast to extinction which shows spontaneous recovery over time.
evaluation: Claims C83-C86 are supported by experimental data showing no spontaneous recovery after MEM treatment (Figures 1A, 2C) and appropriate citations for extinction showing spontaneous recovery (C84). The distinction between forgetting and extinction is important for mechanistic understanding and potential therapeutic applications. The inference (C86) is reasonable given the data.

result: Forgetting is a targetable process for PTSD treatment. Interventions that promote forgetting may represent an alternative or adjunct approach to extinction and reconsolidation-based therapies for modifying traumatic memories.
evaluation: Claims C88, C95, C103, C112 represent speculative translational implications. While the basic science findings are solid, the leap to PTSD treatment is not directly tested. The authors appropriately use cautious language ('may contribute,' 'potentially viable'), but no clinical data or PTSD models are presented. The claims are reasonable speculation but lack direct experimental support in the manuscript.

result: Background claims establishing that: (1) MEM is an NMDA receptor antagonist, (2) MEM enhances hippocampal neurogenesis and forgetting, (3) neurogenesis persists in adult hippocampus and SVZ, and (4) increasing/decreasing neurogenesis accelerates/stabilizes forgetting.
evaluation: Claims C1, C6-C7, C12, C96-C98 are background claims supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These establish the foundation for the current study. The citations appear accurate and comprehensive. These are not novel findings of this study but important context.

result: Background claims on fear memory processes: extinction is an inhibitory learning process preserving original memory; reconsolidation involves retrieval-induced destabilization requiring protein synthesis; forgetting can weaken memories; PTSD interventions have focused on extinction and reconsolidation; fear conditioning creates CS-US associations consolidated through gene expression.
evaluation: Claims C89-C94, C104-C105 accurately summarize established knowledge about fear memory processes with appropriate citations. These provide essential background for understanding the novelty and significance of the current findings. The characterizations are consistent with the cited literature.

result: Summary claim: Increases in hippocampal neurogenesis promote forgetting of hippocampus-dependent recent memory, but not remote and/or hippocampus-independent memory (without reminders).
evaluation: Claim C50 is a summary inference integrating findings from multiple experiments (Figures 1-2). It accurately captures the pattern of results showing specificity for hippocampus-dependent recent memories. This sets up the key question of whether reminders can restore susceptibility of remote memories.

result: Most approaches to weaken or erase fear memory target reconsolidation and extinction of recent, but not remote, memory - representing a major challenge for PTSD treatment.
evaluation: Claim C102 accurately characterizes a limitation in the field with appropriate citations. This establishes the clinical motivation for the current work on remote memory modification. The characterization is consistent with the cited literature and represents an important gap the study addresses.
